analysis.one_liner: Requires political groups to report their money monthly before elections and lets the IRS and FEC share the data publicly.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it was referred to two House committees in February 2005 and died there when the Congress ended in January 2007, with no cosponsors and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Section 527 political organizations — tax-exempt groups that spend money to influence elections — currently report their finances much less often. This bill would have required monthly reports in election years for groups raising or spending $25,000 or more, quarterly reports for smaller groups, and special pre- and post-election reports, plus twice-yearly reports in off years [S2][S3]. It also would have directed the Treasury Department and the Federal Election Commission to link their disclosure databases and make political money records easier for the public to search, with reports to Congress on progress [S2][S3]. The bill was introduced by Rep. John Larson with no cosponsors, referred to the Ways and Means and House Administration committees, and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action [S1][S4][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Voters, journalists, and watchdog groups who want to see who is bankrolling election-season political advertising before they vote, rather than months after; the bill's more frequent filings and unified searchable databases are aimed at making that possible [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Groups raising or spending $25,000 or more in an election year would have filed reports monthly, with a pre-election report due 12 days before each election they participate in, so donors could be seen before the vote rather than long after [S3].

The Treasury Secretary and the FEC would have been required to connect their public disclosure databases so that a person could follow the same political money across both agencies' records, and each agency would have had to report its progress to Congress [S3].

Smaller organizations would have filed quarterly, but any group crossing the $25,000 line would have shifted to monthly reporting, closing a gap in which large late money could move without timely disclosure [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Section 527 political organizations and their donors would bear the cost of more frequent, more detailed reporting, and taxpayers would fund the Treasury and FEC work to upgrade and link the disclosure databases, which the bill authorizes in 'such sums as may be necessary' [S3].

drawbacks.text: Monthly reporting, pre-election reports due 12 days before an election, and separate post-election filings add real paperwork and compliance costs for political organizations, and small groups that cross the $25,000 threshold mid-year would have had to retroactively file monthly reports for the earlier months [S3].

The database-linkage provisions are directives to two agencies with an open-ended authorization of funds and a July 2005 interim report deadline, so the bill depended on agencies executing a technically difficult systems project on a short timeline [S3].

Disclosure alone does not limit the money itself: the bill would have made political spending more visible but placed no limits on contributions, expenditures, or the organizations' activities [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is meaningful but modest: faster, better-linked disclosure of 527-group money helps voters and journalists see who funds election-season advertising, at the price of more reporting work for political organizations and modest agency spending on database integration [S2][S3]. The design is reasonable — the $25,000 threshold spares the smallest groups — but disclosure-only reform leaves the underlying money flows untouched [S2]. The larger problem for this bill was never its design; it was that it never moved.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to two House committees, neither ever took it up, and it died there when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. John Larson of Connecticut introduced the bill on February 1, 2005, with no cosponsors [S1][S4][S5].

The Speaker referred it to the Ways and Means Committee, which has jurisdiction over the tax-code disclosure provisions, and to the House Administration Committee, which handles election law, with no action recorded in either [S5].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action appears in the bill's complete action history through the end of the 109th Congress on January 3, 2007 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Section 527 political organizations and their large donors, who avoided more frequent public reporting of their election spending, and the incumbent officeholders those groups support, who kept the existing slower disclosure rules.

for.name: Rep. John Larson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its only sponsor; no other member signed on.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over the tax-code disclosure provisions (Chair: Bill Thomas, R-CA)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral covering the bill's core reporting amendments and took no recorded action on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Committee on House Administration
against.role: Second committee of referral, with jurisdiction over election-related disclosure (Chair: Bob Ney, R-OH)
against.what_they_did: Received a referral of the bill and recorded no hearing, markup, or vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, so it never generated enough support to reveal a partisan split [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have forced monthly and pre-election reporting of contributions and expenditures, shrinking the window in which large political money could move without public visibility. Their interest in slower disclosure runs against voters' interest in seeing the money before an election [S3].
Monthly reports and pre-election filings would have exposed donor names and amounts weeks earlier than current law requires. Avoiding that timing cost is why the status quo favored them [S3].

industries.industry: Campaign compliance and disclosure software vendors
industries.note: More frequent filings and mandated improvements to the Treasury and FEC databases would have created work for firms that help organizations file and that build public disclosure systems. A small, indirect beneficiary [S3].
